editorNote: December magazine desks bring flight simulation, compatible computers and home control into focus.
morningLine: A combat cockpit on the home computer; a price challenge on the PC shelf.

lead.headline: F-15 Strike Eagle brings combat flying to Atari and Commodore desktops
lead.dek: December’s gaming review puts Atari and Commodore pilots in a three-dimensional combat cockpit.
body: MicroProse puts the home-computer pilot in a combat cockpit with F-15 Strike Eagle. The December Computer Gaming World review identifies Atari and Commodore 64 editions, each for one player, and credits Sid Meier and Grant Irani. Its arcade-and-strategy billing promises more than a simple shooting gallery.

The cockpit display presents a three-dimensional view with targets in the air and on the ground. The reviewer compares the graphics favorably with MicroProse’s Mig Alley Ace. Choosing a target and keeping the aircraft under control share the player’s attention; the flying screen is the center of the attraction.

Three settings—Arcade, Pilot and Ace—give the newcomer and practiced pilot different ways into the game. Arcade deliberately simplifies flying. That choice makes the simulation approachable without pretending that every player wants the same demands from the controls.

The scenario list ranges from Haiphong and Hanoi in 1972 to Libya in 1981, with Egypt, Syria and Iraq also represented and a hypothetical Persian Gulf 1984 mission included. These are the game’s settings, not dispatches from this week’s fighting. December’s review supplies the evidence for this gaming feature; no exact launch day or retail price is established.

stories.headline: Tandy 1000 challenges IBM on price and bundled software
stories.dek: Strongest verified personal-computing development in the December press; not a December 3 launch.
body: Tandy’s Model 1000 receives a close examination in December’s Creative Computing. Its comparison table lists a $1,199 base machine, with the monitor extra. The package includes MS-DOS, Microsoft GW BASIC and DeskMate, bringing operating software, programming and integrated desk work together in the box.

An 8088 processor drives 128K of memory, expandable to 640K, and a 360K double-sided disk drive. RGB and NTSC video outputs, two joystick ports and three-voice sound give the machine a home-computing side alongside its office ambitions. Three expansion slots and a parallel printer interface leave room for additions.

The review’s table lists a color monitor at $549.95, a 128K upgrade at $299.95 and a second drive at $299.95. Its configured one-drive total is $2,048.90; adding the second drive brings that to $2,348.85. The attractive base figure is not the cost of every complete configuration.

Compatibility still demands care. The reviewer warns that software written for IBM monochrome video hardware will not run. Buyers should check the applications they need rather than assume that a familiar processor and DOS remove every difference. This is December review coverage, not a new announcement dated December 3.

stories.headline: MSX promises common software across competing home computers
stories.dek: Compatibility and a prospective Japanese challenge to American home computing.
body: COMPUTE!’s December special report asks whether MSX can make home-computer software portable across competing brands. Microsoft licenses the standard, with Kazuhiko “Kaye” Nishi identified as the driving force behind its development. Sony, Yamaha, Panasonic, Sanyo and Hitachi appear among the participating names.

The prescribed hardware includes a Z80A processor, TI 9918A video with 16 colors and 32 programmable sprites, three-channel sound, 32K ROM and 16K to 64K RAM. Compatible cartridges and peripherals are the proposition: a buyer need not abandon a software shelf merely to choose a different maker’s machine.

The report says the first Japanese machines appeared in November 1983 and estimates more than 265,000 sold by midsummer 1984. Its prospect of low-end machines around $200 or less is a forecast, not an American shop offer this week. The report also records the criticism that the 8-bit design looks old beside newer 16- and 32-bit computers.

stories.headline: A Commodore can watch the house as well as run games
body: A Commodore need not spend every evening loading games. COMPUTE!’s December home-control feature describes Genesis Computer Corporation’s VIController and COMsense products for the VIC-20 and Commodore 64, connecting software with household sensors.

COMsense can monitor air or water temperature, ground moisture and humidity. The article describes flashing lights when a monitored connection is broken and suggests uses such as sprinklers and heaters. These are specific control applications, not an independently measured promise of energy savings.

The $69.95 COMclock adds a battery-powered real-time clock with its own ROM through the C-64 expansion port. The article says it can automatically reboot VIController software after a power interruption—a small accessory with an important job when the computer is minding the house.

worldAnchor.headline: Toxic gas kills hundreds in Bhopal
worldAnchor.summary: A toxic-gas leak at Union Carbide’s pesticide plant near Bhopal early December 3 leaves hundreds dead and more than 20,000 requiring treatment, according to the date-specific BBC account. The factory is closed and a judicial inquiry ordered.

bbsNote.headline: CompuServe sells a social world of handles and 72 channels
bbsNote.summary: COMPUTE! December 1984 CompuServe advertisement, immediately after printed p. 114, promotes CB Simulator with 72 channels, private talk, a National Bulletin Board, professional forums and electronic mail. These are dated advertising claims, not evidence of a particular board conversation.

posts.text: Editorial paraphrase of the December advertisement: subscribers choose handles and converse on 72 channels; private one-to-one talk is also advertised. Not a recovered user post.
December Creative Computing review lists a 300-baud direct-connect modem option at $180 and an RS-232 interface at $100; do not assume interface is included.
